You are a research assistant answering questions about a fixed set of papers.
The papers are plain-text files in your working directory. Explore them with the tools:
- bash: read-only shell (ls, grep -n, find, head, tail, wc, nl, cat, sed -n 'A,Bp')
- read(path, offset, limit): read a file with line numbers

Rules:
- Answer ONLY from text you have actually read in this session. Do not answer from memory.
- If the papers do not contain the answer, say so explicitly instead of guessing.
- When you have enough evidence, reply with your final answer and make NO tool call.
- Support every factual claim with a verbatim quote copied exactly from the source, in the form: "exact text" (file). Never paraphrase inside the quotation marks. A statement that the document(s) do not contain the requested information needs no citation.
- State only what the document(s) say. Do not add background knowledge, general advice, or your own
  conclusions. If the user asks for something the text only partly covers, answer the covered part
  and say plainly which part the document does not address.
- Do not expand abbreviations, name entities, or add details that the text itself does not give.
- Do not end with a summary that recombines earlier points ("In short", "Overall"); the points stand on their own.
- When the user describes their own situation, say what the document states that applies to it; do not
  draw a personal conclusion that the document does not state itself.
- After you give an answer, an automatic check verifies your citations. If you then receive a
  <verification> message, you are in revision mode: fix ONLY the flagged problems by calling
  edit_draft(old, new), where `old` is an exact, unique substring of your previous answer.
  Keep everything else unchanged, and reply "Done" when finished.
  Never call edit_draft before you have given an answer.

230	By the fifteenth century, demand for coffee had increased so much that the harvest of
   231	berries from the wild was not enough, and thus in Yemen, people began to plant coffee.
   232	Following Yemen’s lead, other Arab countries also started coffee plantations. Until the
   233	seventeenth century, coffee was cultivated only within North African and Arab countries.
   234	Arabs were very protective of their monopoly on the coffee trade. The cultivation of coffee
   235	and the processing of seeds was a mystery to the world outside of Arabia. Foreigners were
   236	not allowed to visit coffee farms, and only roasted coffee beans (incapable of producing new
   237	plants) were exported. Around 1600, Baba Budan, a Sufi who was on the Haj pilgrimage,
   238	successfully smuggled seven coffee seeds into India and started a small coffee nursery
   239	in Mysore. The early coffee plantations of South India used propagations of plants from
   240	Budan’s garden.
   241	In 1616, a Dutch spy also succeeded in stealing coffee beans from Arabia, and these were
   242	used by the Dutch East India Company as starters for coffee plantations in Java, Sumatra,
   243	Bali, Sri Lanka, Timur, and Suriname (Dutch Guiana). In 1706, a coffee plant from Java was
   244	brought to the botanic gardens of Amsterdam, and from there, its offspring reached Jardin
   245	de plantes in Paris. A clone of the Parisian plant was sent to the French colony Martinique,
   246	and then its offspring spread to the French colonies in the Caribbean, South America, and
   247	Africa. In 1728, a Portuguese officer from Dutch Guiana brought coffee seeds to Brazil,
   248	60 | Colonial Agriculture
   249	which served as starters for the coffee plantations there. The Portuguese also introduced
   250	coffee to African countries and Indonesia, and the British established plantations in their
   251	Caribbean colonies, India, and Sri Lanka from Dutch stock.
   252	In summary, all European coffee plants came from the same Arabian mother plant. So
   253	the biodiversity within their coffee plantations was almost zero, which had devastating
   254	consequences. In the last decades of the nineteenth century, the fungal pathogen
   255	Haemilia vestatrix severely infected coffee plantations in Sri Lanka, India, Java, Sumatra,
   256	and Malaysia. As a result, rust disease destroyed the coffee plantations one by one. Later, in
   257	some of the coffee plantations, Coffea canephora (syn. Coffea robusta), which has a natural
   258	resistance to rust, was planted, but others were converted into tea plantations (as in the
   259	case of Sri Lanka, discussed earlier).
   260	European coffee plantations used the same model as tea or sugar plantations, and so
   261	their workers lived under the same conditions. European powers forcefully employed the
   262	poor native population in these plantations and used indentured laborers as needed. For
   263	example, in Sri Lanka, the Sinhalese population refused to work in the coffee farms, so
   264	British planters recruited 100,000 indentured Tamil workers from India to work the farms
   265	and tea plantations there.
   266	3.7 The Heritage of Plantations
   267	In the twentieth century, most former European colonies became independent countries.
   268	In these countries, private, cooperative, or semigovernmental institutions manage
   269	plantations of sugarcane, tea, coffee, or other commercial crops. Though these plantations
   270	remain a significant source of revenue and contribute significantly to the national GDP of
   271	many countries, their workers still often operate under abject conditions.
   272	References
   273	Johannessen, C. L., & Sorenson, J. L. (2009). World trade and biological exchanges before
   274	1492. iUniverse. (↵ Return)
